blocks.text: Imagine reading a sentence and trying to understand its structure by starting from the end. This is the essence of bottom-up parsing in compilers.

blocks.markdown: Bottom-up parsing is a strategy for analyzing the syntax of a string by attempting to construct a parse tree from the leaves (input tokens) up to the root (start symbol). It is a key technique in compiler design, particularly for constructing parsers that can handle a wide range of grammars.

blocks.title: Shift-Reduce Parsing
blocks.text: Shift-reduce parsing is a type of bottom-up parsing that uses a stack to hold grammar symbols and an input buffer for the remaining input tokens. The parser shifts tokens onto the stack and reduces them using grammar rules.

blocks.markdown: In shift-reduce parsing, the parser uses two main operations: **shift**, which moves the next input token onto the stack, and **reduce**, which replaces a sequence of symbols on the stack with a non-terminal according to a grammar rule. The parser continues these operations until it constructs the start symbol of the grammar.

blocks.markdown: Shift-reduce parsers can be implemented using LR parsing techniques, which are more powerful than LL parsers. LR parsers can handle a larger class of grammars, including those with left recursion and certain types of ambiguity.

blocks.title: LR Parsing
blocks.text: LR parsers are a type of bottom-up parser that can handle a wider range of context-free grammars than LL parsers. They are more powerful because they use a more sophisticated lookahead mechanism and can manage left recursion.

blocks.markdown: One common issue in shift-reduce parsing is the presence of **shift-reduce conflicts**, which occur when the parser can either shift the next input token or reduce the stack contents according to a grammar rule. These conflicts need to be resolved to ensure correct parsing.
